steps.tx: A **warm autoimmune haemolytic anaemia** is the most common form of immune-mediated hemolytic disease, accounting for seventy to eighty percent of all autoimmune haemolytic anaemias. It is mediated by warm-reactive IgG autoantibodies, with optimal binding affinity at normal core body temperature (thirty-seven degrees Celsius). These autoantibodies are characteristically directed against pan-antigenic determinants of the Rh blood group complex.
steps.say: Warm autoimmune haemolytic anaemia accounts for three-quarters of all immune haemolytic anaemias. It is caused by IgG autoantibodies that bind optimally at core body temperature of thirty-seven degrees. These antibodies usually target Rh blood group antigens on the red cell surface, triggering rapid immune destruction.

vis.alt: Diagram illustrating IgG autoantibody opsonization of erythrocytes and partial phagocytosis by splenic macrophages.
vis.caption: IgG opsonization and partial splenic macrophage phagocytosis producing microspherocytes.

steps.tx: The central mechanism of erythrocyte clearance is extravascular **splenic macrophage phagocytosis**. Red cells opsonized with IgG pass through the splenic cords of Billroth. Splenic red pulp macrophages recognize the Fc portions of bound IgG via Fc-gamma receptors and phagocytose portions of the erythrocyte membrane. The red cell seals without losing intracellular volume, forcing it to assume a rigid, spherical shape.
steps.say: Red cells coated with IgG travel into the red pulp of the spleen. Splenic macrophages latch onto the IgG tail using Fc receptors and take bites out of the cell membrane. The damaged cell seals itself up without losing volume, progressively morphing from a flexible biconcave disc into a rigid microspherocyte.

vis.title: Warm versus Cold Autoimmune Haemolytic Anaemia

steps.tx: The peripheral blood smear demonstrates prominent **microspherocytes** accompanied by polychromasia reflecting robust compensatory reticulocytosis. Microspherocytes appear as small, intensely stained, hyperchromic spherical erythrocytes lacking central pallor. Unlike hereditary spherocytosis where spherocytes are uniform, warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia displays spherocytes of varying sizes intermixed with polychromatophilic reticulocytes and nucleated red blood cells.
steps.say: On the blood film, look for microspherocytes and polychromasia. Microspherocytes are small, dense, dark pink spheres without any central pallor. Unlike the uniform spherocytes in genetic disease, autoimmune spherocytes vary widely in size and sit alongside large bluish-grey reticulocytes and nucleated red cells.

left.title: Warm AIHA Smear Findings
points: Nucleated red blood cells under severe stress
Elevated MCHC (>36 g/dL) due to dehydration

right.title: Biochemical Haemolysis Markers
points: Normal or slightly increased urinary urobilinogen

steps.tx: The diagnostic cornerstone is the **direct antiglobulin test**, historically designated the Coombs test. The patient washed red blood cells are incubated with antihuman globulin (Coombs reagent containing antibodies to human IgG and complement C3d). In warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia, addition of the reagent cross-links surface-bound IgG autoantibodies, producing macroscopic agglutination. A positive direct test confirms immune-mediated opsonization in vivo.
steps.say: The direct Coombs test is the gold standard investigation. The laboratory takes the patient washed red blood cells and mixes them with antihuman globulin. If the red cells are coated with IgG autoantibodies in the bloodstream, the Coombs reagent bridges them together, causing visible clumping.

steps.tx: First-line medical therapy mandates high-dose **corticosteroid therapy** with oral prednisone (one to one point five milligrams per kilogram daily). Corticosteroids downregulate Fc-gamma receptor expression on splenic macrophages, suppressing erythrocyte clearance within twenty-four to seventy-two hours, while gradually tapering autoantibody synthesis. In refractory cases, the anti-CD20 monoclonal antibody rituximab eradicates pathogenic B-lymphocyte clones, while splenectomy removes the primary filtration bed.
steps.say: Treat warm AIHA with high-dose oral prednisone. Steroids rapidly downregulate Fc receptors on splenic macrophages, halting red cell destruction within one to three days, while slowing down antibody production. If steroids fail, rituximab wipes out the responsible B cell clones, or splenectomy removes the filter where destruction occurs.

left.title: First-Line Prednisone
points: Requires slow taper over 6 to 12 months

right.title: Second-Line Modalities
points: Splenectomy: removes primary site of destruction
Folic acid supplementation (1 to 5 mg daily)

quiz.q: Which immunoglobulin class and thermal optimum characterize the autoantibodies in warm autoimmune haemolytic anaemia?
options: IgG with optimal reactivity at 37 degrees Celsius
IgM with optimal reactivity at 0 to 4 degrees Celsius
IgA with optimal reactivity at 20 degrees Celsius
IgE with optimal reactivity at 42 degrees Celsius
quiz.explain: Warm AIHA is mediated by IgG autoantibodies (optimally active at 37 degrees Celsius) directed against Rh complex antigens, causing splenic extravascular haemolysis.

quiz.q: What is the primary cellular mechanism by which microspherocytes are generated in warm AIHA?
options: Partial phagocytosis of IgG-coated membrane by splenic macrophages
Complement membrane attack complex (C5b-9) osmotic lysis
Spontaneous loss of spectrin dimers through renal filtration
Oxidative cross-linking of haemoglobin to the band 3 anion exchanger
quiz.explain: Splenic macrophages recognize the Fc portion of IgG on red blood cells and phagocytose portions of the membrane; the red cell reseals with decreased surface area, forming a microspherocyte.
